analysis.one_liner: Requires government agencies to pay landowners cash whenever regulation cuts a property's value by 10% or $10,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote; it sat in the Judiciary Committee's Constitution subcommittee until the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced federal agencies—and state agencies carrying out federally mandated programs—to pay property owners whenever a government decision lowered a property's value by as little as 10% or $10,000, restricted most of its use, or attached conditions to a permit. Compensation would come out of agency budgets or a federal judgment fund, and the government would bear the burden of proving its rules were justified in most disputes. It also consolidated property-rights lawsuits into a single court of the owner's choosing and gave winning owners their attorney fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of regulated land—most substantially owners of large or valuable parcels such as developers, ranchers, and timber, mining, and energy interests—would receive cash compensation for any regulation that reduced their property's value past the low threshold, plus attorney and expert-witness fees if they won, and could choose the friendlier of two federal courts [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Owners of regulated land and developers

how_it_helps.text: A property owner would be owed compensation if a government action physically invaded property, failed to substantially advance the government's stated purpose, forced an unwanted dedication as a permit condition, wiped out substantially all productive use, or cut the affected property's value by 10% or $10,000 [S2] [S3].
The government, not the owner, would bear the burden of proof on most claims, and compensation would include business losses and compounded interest from the date of the taking [S2] [S3].

Owners could sue in either U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims, ending the old rule that forced them to choose between one court for money damages and another to strike down the regulation; winning plaintiffs would recover attorney and expert fees [S2] [S3].
State agencies enforcing federally mandated programs would be covered, and the United States would waive sovereign immunity so owners could sue directly [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the budgets of the regulating agency or the federal Judgment Fund, and the public more broadly, because routine environmental, land-use, and safety rules would become a cash liability for the government, making such rules far more expensive—or impossible—to issue or enforce [S3].

drawbacks.text: The trigger is very low—any regulation that reduces the affected property's value by 10% or $10,000 would create a right to compensation—so ordinary protections like wetland rules, endangered-species restrictions, or zoning conditions could generate payouts from public funds [S2] [S3].

Compensation would be paid out of the regulating agency's own budget or the Judgment Fund, meaning every new environmental or land-use rule would carry an open-ended price tag paid by taxpayers, and the government would have to prove a landowner's use is a nuisance to escape paying [S3].
The bill applies retroactively in effect from January 1, 1995, covering agency actions occurring after that date regardless of when the underlying rules were adopted [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill contains a real procedural improvement—letting owners pursue money and equitable relief in one court instead of being bounced between two—but that reform is overshadowed by a compensation mandate so broad that nearly any regulation touching property value would require payment. The practical effect would be to make environmental, health, and land-use protections prohibitively expensive to enforce, with the bill's own findings framing the cost of public protections as something taxpayers must instead pay to individual landowners [S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Constitution subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lamar Smith of Texas introduced the bill on January 11, 1995, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
On January 25, 1995, it was referred to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on the Constitution, where no further action was taken [S5].
The action history notes 'For Further Action See H.R.925,' indicating the House pursued the property-rights issue through a separate, broader bill instead [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still in subcommittee and no vote ever taken [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, taxpayers were spared a new open-ended obligation to pay landowners for the effects of ordinary regulation, and agencies retained the ability to issue environmental, land-use, and safety rules without a compensation price tag. The procedural court-access reform it offered was also lost.

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as restoring Fifth Amendment just-compensation rights for property owners [S1] [S3].

for.name: 27 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, along with 1 of 204 House Democrats [S4].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 11, 1995, sent it to the Constitution subcommittee on January 25, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House leadership and committee chairs of the 104th Congress
against.what_they_did: Prioritized a separate, broader property-rights bill (H.R. 925) over this one, which never advanced beyond subcommittee referral [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was almost entirely Republican—27 of 28 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democratic cosponsor [S4].

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large landowners
industries.note: The bill would convert regulatory restrictions on their land into cash payments from the federal treasury, with the government bearing the burden of proof and winners collecting attorney fees. The money would come from agency budgets and the federal Judgment Fund—that is, from taxpayers.

industries.industry: Timber, mining, oil and gas, and agricultural interests
industries.note: These industries hold extensive land subject to federal environmental and land-use rules; the bill's low 10% or $10,000 value-diminution trigger would make many such restrictions compensable at public expense.

industries.industry: Federal and state regulatory agencies (environmental, land-use, health and safety)
industries.note: Agencies would pay compensation out of their own appropriations for actions that reduce property values, effectively pricing their protective mission out of reach; state agencies enforcing federally mandated programs would be covered too.
